video.title: AI Lets You Start This Amazon Side Hustle in Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates how to research, create and publish AI-assisted books through Amazon KDP, with BookBolt as the main research and formatting tool. The examples include coloring books, journals, activity books and puzzle books, alongside second-hand case studies with reported sales. He recommends looking for specific demand, checking competition, and customizing templates rather than publishing generic material. The key takeaway is to treat early books as experiments: test consistently, learn from results and build on the products that find buyers.

ideas.one_liner: Publish ebooks and print-on-demand books on Amazon, using research and AI tools to choose topics and create book content.

ideas.customer: Amazon shoppers searching for books, journals, coloring books and other book products.
ideas.problem: Readers want useful or entertaining books on specific topics; publishers need to identify demand and make books that match it.
ideas.offer: Books published on Amazon, including ebooks and print-on-demand books; AI can help produce content, while the publisher researches and edits the product.

pricing.notes: Other prices in the transcript refer to individual examples and are recorded under those ideas.

acquisition_channels.details: Publish on Amazon KDP and use relevant book titles and keywords so shoppers can find the books. The host suggests adding Amazon ads after finding a winning book.

acquisition_channels.details: The host proposes Amazon ads for products that show promise; no campaign setup or results are described.

quote.text: Then once you find a winner, then you can put Amazon ads behind it.

ideas.delivery: The publisher creates and uploads book files through KDP. Amazon sells ebooks and handles printing and fulfilment for print books; the publisher does not take possession of or ship physical stock.
unit_economics_claims: Shannon is reported to earn thousands of dollars per month from Amazon book payments.
The host gives a hypothetical example of $3 royalty per copy and 10 copies per day.
The host says the business can become relatively passive after the initial work, but gives no verified results for his own books.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. A hypothetical example uses $20 per month for research software and another $20 per month for AI software.

acquisition.how: Marketplace listings and ads can bring inbound buyers, but a person must choose topics, assess demand and manage advertising.

onboarding.how: AI can help draft and format material, while a person must choose the niche, review the content and prepare the listing.

delivery.how: KDP can deliver ebooks and print and fulfil physical books after upload; the publisher still creates and checks the files.

billing.how: Amazon processes customer payments and royalties; the publisher may need to monitor accounts and statements.

support.how: The host says there is no customer support or shipping work for the publisher; account and content issues may still need human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: The KDP publishing model can be adapted for UK readers, but the publisher would need to research UK demand, choose UK-relevant topics and account for local pricing and marketplace differences.

risks: The host says many publishers do not find the success they want and warns that the first book may not be good.
Poor niche research, oversaturated topics and generic designs may lead to weak sales.
AI-generated text or artwork may need careful human review for accuracy, quality and originality.
The cited case studies are not representative guarantees of earnings.

tactics.name: Use marketplace research before choosing a book topic
steps: Start with a topic you know well enough to edit and judge.
Use BookBolt keyword and product research to compare search interest, competition and estimated sales.
Try specific long-tail phrases rather than broad topics alone.
Check whether searchers appear to want books; the host notes that Texas barbecue searches may be restaurant searches.
Look at movers-and-shakers and evergreen product lists for ideas, then validate the niche further.

quote.text: the more specific and niche your keywords are the better your search results will be.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Choose a topic the publisher can review
steps: List topics the publisher knows and cares about.
Use that familiarity to review AI-written material and spot content that does not make sense.
Do not assume AI removes the need for subject knowledge or editing.

quote.text: we need to be able to edit it so the book or piece of content reads in a way that just makes sense, that doesn't sound like AI.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Differentiate and test journal titles
steps: Study existing journal titles and identify a clear, relatable angle.
Use ChatGPT to brainstorm related title ideas.
Publish a small batch of ideas to learn which gets traction.
Customize templates rather than using default output unchanged.

quote.text: Give me 10 more journal ideas with funny titles like these.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Put advertising behind products that show signs of demand
steps: Publish and test products first.
Identify a product that appears to be a winner.
Then put Amazon ads behind that product.

quote.text: Then once you find a winner, then you can put Amazon ads behind it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use BookBolt Studio to prepare KDP-ready files
steps: Choose a journal size and interior format.
Set the paper type and page count.
Use the studio's formatting for Amazon KDP, then review the design before publishing.

quote.text: the studio formats everything in the right way for Amazon KDP. So, you don't have to do all this work twice.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Run a short initial experiment and keep learning
steps: Try the process for 30 days.
Start with one product to learn the workflow.
Then test other product types such as coloring books, planners, calendars and graduation guest books.
Treat the first book as practice rather than assuming it will be a winner.

quote.text: Start by trying this for 30 days. Start by testing one product just to see how it works.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Research demand and competition before spending substantial time making a product.

quote.text: We really need keyword research tools so we could know what to spend our time on before we actually dive way into it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Specific long-tail searches can reveal opportunities that broad keywords hide, but search intent still needs checking.

quote.text: If you're willing to put a little bit of legwork in, you will get a lot more results out of that legwork.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Use templates to get started, then customize the product so it is distinct and useful.

quote.text: You got to customize your templates. Don't just give what the software spits out to you. You got to make it different, cute, unique, etc.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Treat the first product as learning and test more than one concept before deciding what works.

quote.text: Your first book is mostly for learning. This is not a get-rich-quick scheme and it's not guaranteed.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Publishing through a marketplace can make fulfilment simpler because the platform handles printing and shipping.

quote.text: There's no customer support. There's nothing to ship, package, returns, tracking, etc.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: An idea is not validated just because its creator likes it; use buyer and sales evidence.

quote.text: Just cuz you think your idea is good doesn't mean that the market does.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: The host presents book publishing as an asymmetric experiment: limited software costs can lead either to a win or to reusable learning.

quote.text: You'll either win or you'll learn and use those same skills in whatever else you launch next.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

evidence_quality.rationale: The host demonstrates BookBolt and explains a research workflow, but most specific sales and earnings figures are estimates from software or second-hand ChatGPT research. The host also acknowledges that success is not typical or guaranteed.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host demonstrates and endorses BookBolt, including its research and formatting tools. No sponsor read is included in the transcript.
